zones.label: Column 1

Used for entry identification, not as a substitute transcription. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Nos completes annos from the preceding page, followed by hours. Tatçuno toqi introduces the dragon-sign time interval; the Portuguese word is horas, not OCR boras.

runs.text: oito peru as noue horas da manhãa.

lines.note: The printed explanation places the interval from eight toward nine in the morning. Enlargement supports the anomalous peru rather than expected pera, and places the tilde in manhãa on the first a after h; retain these local readings rather than the reference notes' general pattern.

runs.text: O ladrar o cão à maneira de lobo

lines.note: Tatçuboye describes a dog's wolf-like howling. The cedilla below c is visible and restores tçu rather than OCR tcu; the prolonged nature of the sound follows below.

runs.text: que voyua continuando por algum eſpaço. No

lines.note: The wolf howls continuously for some time. No begins a regional usage qualification continued on the next physical line.

In the Cami region the expression is Nagaboye. Both are Japanese terms embedded in the Portuguese sentence. Enlargement shows Nagaboye in italic, with sloping single-storey a forms contrasting with the upright Japanese examples; it is not a separate headword.

runs.text: Cabeça de lagarto, que poẽ por

lines.note: Tatçugaxira names a dragon- or lizard-head ornament. The source's literal Cabeça de lagarto is retained, with its placement on helmets explained below.
The head is put on a helmet's crest as an ornament. This indented continuation completes Tatçugaxira rather than introducing another equipment term.
Tatçumi is the direction between east and south, explicitly Figaxito Minamino ai. The Japanese directional explanation is a synonym phrase, not an embedded Portuguese term.
Sueſte completes the Portuguese direction, southeast. It remains a separate short physical row under the preceding headword.
Tatçuni and tateni are adverbial alternatives meaning lengthwise. Preserve the printed tçu in the first form rather than harmonizing it with the second.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de rodela que ſe aßenta

lines.note: Tate is a shield or defensive screen that is set down. The following lines explain its ground-supported military use rather than a handheld circular shield alone.

runs.text: no chão como repairo de que vſão na guerra os

lines.note: The screen is placed on the ground as protection in war. Preserve repairo and vſão as the source's historical spellings, with the users identified below.
Iapões identifies the users; Tateuo tçuqu then illustrates keeping the shield in position. The translation's ro- begins rodela across the next row.

runs.text: dela, ou repairo poſto contra as ſetas, ou pi-

lines.note: Dela completes rodela, the shield or defensive screen placed against arrows or shot. The final pi- is the beginning of pilouros below.
Louros completes pilouros, projectiles or shot. This short line closes the military shield example, not the following dimensional sense of Tate.
Tate or tateſama denotes the lengthwise dimension of a figure or object. The damaged g descender remains visible in dalgũa, correcting the OCR's false internal gap.

runs.text: ra, ou outra couſa que tem traueſa, ou largu-

lines.note: Ra completes figura, and the object is said also to have a crosswise dimension or breadth. This contrast explains tate relationally rather than as an absolute size.
Ra completes largura. The short closing row belongs to the length-versus-width definition and has no independent Japanese material.
Tate introduces the verb to raise or set up. Qi begins the first example, paired with faxira on the following row; Vt is part of the italic apparatus.
Faxirauo tatçuru means erecting posts or pillars. The Portuguese gives paos and then the Japanese-derived plural Faxiras, divided Fa-/xiras across the line break.
Xiras completes the pillar term; Chauo tatçuru then means preparing tea. The Portuguese verb is Concertar, with t rather than OCR i, and its object follows below.

The tea is prepared in porcelain, followed by the oath example Xeimonuo tatçuru. The final vowel of the printed porſolano looks like o; retain this local spelling rather than silently substituting expected porſolana.
Iurar, to swear an oath, translates Xeimonuo tatçuru; it is not OCR Furar, to pierce. Zonbunuo tatçuru then introduces maintaining one's own opinion.
Sustaining one's opinion completes Zonbunuo tatçuru. Farano tatçu- begins the anger expression; preserve the printed no rather than substituting an expected object particle.
Ru completes Farano tatçuru, becoming angry. Fizauo tatçuru then introduces a kneeling posture, with the Portuguese Por- continuing into Porſe below.

runs.text: ſe de joelhos ao modo de Iapão. ¶

lines.note: The posture is explained as kneeling in the Japanese manner. Guãuo begins making a vow; the visible tilde over a abbreviates the nasal and must not be omitted as in OCR Guauo.
Tatçuru completes the vow example, translated Fazer votos. Monouo me- then begins placing something before one's eyes, continued below.

runs.text: Por diante dos olhos algũa cou-

lines.note: Ni completes meni, before the eyes. The Portuguese begins putting something in view; keep the attached Japanese particles and the physical cou-/ſa division.
The object is placed so that it may be seen. Mon or to are then alternative Japanese words for a gate or door in the next example.

runs.text: Fechar a porta da rua, ou outra por

lines.note: Tçuru completes the door-closing example. The Portuguese distinguishes the street door from another door, with porta continuing without an added hyphen across the row boundary.
Ta completes porta; Miſouo tatçuru then means dissolving or thinning miso. The final Miſo is embedded in the Portuguese sentence and is a word-level typeface candidate.
Nauo tatçuru is glossed as defaming or speaking ill. Restore the visible paragraph mark before the example; do not replace this adverse sense with a modern favourable reading of establishing a name.
Qeixeiuo tatçuru is explained as practising prostitution. The source's molher publica is a historical expression, divided mo-/lher across the next row.
Lher completes the preceding gloss. Tçucaiuo tatçuru introduces sending a message or messenger, with the translation's Man- beginning Mandar.
Dar completes Mandar recado. Xônin or xôcouo tatçu- introduces bringing witnesses or furnishing evidence; the two circumflexes remain distinct printed marks.
Ru completes the witness example. The gloss offers bringing witnesses or giving testimony; the final divided word is teſtemu-, with u rather than OCR a before nho below.
Nho completes teſtemunho. Fanauo tatçuru introduces arranging flowers, translated putting roses; preserve the source's more specific Portuguese flower word.
The flowers are placed like a bouquet in a vessel. Vma- begins the next example, concerning a horse rather than another flower arrangement.

runs.text: Por o caualo preſo na eſtre-

lines.note: Uo completes Vmauo tatçuru, keeping a horse tied in a stable. The Portuguese stable word is divided eſtre-/baria across the next row.
Baria completes eſtrebaria. Ichiuo tatçuru then means holding or setting up a fair or market, another institutional use of the verb.
Fǒuo tatçuru is making or establishing law. The visible o-mark points downward as a caron and is retained independently of the differently marked doctrine example below.
Iyeuo tatçuru is building houses. Fô- begins the next example; its circumflex is visible and must not be harmonized with the preceding Fǒ.
Uo completes Fôuo tatçuru, raising or promulgating a doctrine. The Portuguese object is completed on the next row, not omitted from the definition.
Doutrina closes the previous example. Yuuo tatçuru introduces boiling water, with fer- beginning the Portuguese feruer across the line boundary.
Uer completes feruer, bringing water to a boil. Camiuo tatçuru then introduces letting hair grow, not the divine Cami sense found on the previous page.
Xar completes Deixar crecer os cabelos. Fariuo tatçuru begins inserting a needle, with the medical purpose continuing into column 2.

runs.text: Meter hũa maneira de agulha, ou alfenete no

lines.note: The object is a kind of needle or pin inserted into the body. The historical medical description continues into column 2, where por mezinha explains its use as a remedy.
The needle is inserted as a remedy, completing column 1. Qirifauo tatçuru then concerns setting a blade's cutting edge: the f supports kiriha, not OCR Qiriſa, and tatçuru replaces tarçuru.

runs.text: Fazer o corte à faca, ou caniuete de Iapão dei-

lines.note: The gloss describes forming the cutting edge of a Japanese knife. Corte has o rather than OCR i; dei- starts the explanatory Deixando on the next row.

runs.text: xando lho hũ tamanino inclinado de hũa bãda.

lines.note: The edge is left slightly inclined to one side. Retain the unusual printed diminutive tamanino and the nasal abbreviations rather than expanding them into a modernized account of sharpening.
Tateai means to oppose or stand against someone. The two caroned principal forms are copied from the print, not normalized from modern conjugation.

Tateauaxe means to encounter others in combat. The principal part would normally be suru, but the tall letter has a short rightward mid-height stroke resembling f; retain the baseline furu as a chosen, nonblocking print-level uncertainty rather than normalize it from morphology.
Tros completes outros pelejando, encountering others while fighting. This short row belongs to Tateauaxe's martial sense.

runs.text: Flores, ou roſas postas em algũ vaſo.

lines.note: Tatebana is flowers or roses arranged in a vessel. The gloss parallels Fanauo tatçuru in column 1, but this line is an independent noun entry.

runs.text: Caua feita, & cortada da parte da

lines.note: Tatebori is a ditch or cutting made on the fortress side. The next rows describe its slope and cut edges, so the definition is not merely any excavated pit.

runs.text: fortaleza de maneira q̃ fique muito a lãborada

lines.note: The fortress-side cutting is made markedly sloping or battered. Preserve the visible spacing and abbreviation in a lãborada rather than silently standardizing this specialist Portuguese construction term.

runs.text: com hũas quinas, ou cantos talhados ao cõprido.

lines.note: The work has edges or corners cut lengthwise. The nasal abbreviations in hũas and cõprido remain as printed, and the line completes the fortification description.

runs.text: Carta que ſe fecha ao comprido do-

lines.note: Tatebumi is a letter closed or folded lengthwise. The headword's middle vowel is e, not OCR o; do- begins the Portuguese dobrandoa below.

runs.text: brandoa, & dando lhe nòs ſò mente nas põtas.

lines.note: Brandoa completes the folding instruction, with knots tied only at the ends. Preserve nòs and the separate ſò mente, rather than normalizing the accents or joining the adverb.
Tatecaſane means to build many houses. The long letter in caſane is ſ, not OCR f; the Japanese compound concerns successive or accumulated building.
Ou fazer muitos edificios restates the construction of many buildings. It completes the preceding compound rather than narrowing it to a single building type.
Tatefa denotes a sect, rule, or institution. Here f represents the Japanese h-series sound; it should not be changed to ſ merely because a nearby word required the reverse correction.
Tategomori means being enclosed or holding out in a defended place. The Portuguese for- begins fortalecido, fortified, on the next row.

runs.text: talecido em algũa fortaleza, ou caſa com val-

lines.note: The refuge may be a fortress or a house protected with defensive works. Preserve the val-/los line break rather than merging the physical rows.
Los completes vallos, followed by tranqueiras, palisades or barriers. These are examples of the defences surrounding the place where someone holds out.
Tategu includes windows, wooden doors, and shutters. The following rows qualify these as removable household fittings rather than structural walls.

runs.text: & outros petrechos ſemelhantes da caſa que ſe

lines.note: Other similar household fittings are included. The relative clause continues below and should not be severed by an inferred entry boundary.

runs.text: podem tirar, ou leuar. ¶ Item, Cordas,

lines.note: The fittings can be removed or carried away. Item then introduces a second sense involving a horse's ropes and harness.

runs.text: ſilha, cabresto, &c. com que o caualo està a

lines.note: Ropes, a girth, and a halter are listed as the horse's equipment. The initial a at the edge begins amarrado on the following row without an invented hyphen.
Marrado completes amarrado, the horse being tied in the stable. The final vowel is o rather than OCR e, agreeing with the horse described above.

runs.text: O por diuerſas couſas, ou cores en-

lines.note: Tatemaje concerns putting varied things or colours together in alternation. The Portuguese en- begins the description of interspersing on the following row.

runs.text: treſachadas como varias penas nas frechas, va-

lines.note: Treſachadas completes entreſachadas: the definition concerns alternating or interspersing things. Varied feathers in arrows are the first example; va- begins varias in the next row.
Rias completes the example of varied stripes in pieces of material. The Japanese example is Tatemajeni: a faint a occupies the OCR's false punctuation and space in Tatem. jeni.
Suru completes the Japanese example, interspersing different colours in this way. The Portuguese begins Entreſachar, with n rather than OCR m; the tall initial of ſuru is retained as long s.
Tatematçuri introduces an auxiliary whose effect is described over the following rows. Verbo que junto a ou- begins the explanation of a verb joined to another verb, not an independent object noun.

runs.text: tro humilha ao que falla, & aleuanta aquelle,

lines.note: The auxiliary humbles the speaker and raises the person addressed. Preserve the source's explicit social contrast rather than recasting it as a general polite ending.

runs.text: com quem ſe falla. ¶ Item, Offerecer, ou

lines.note: Com quem ſe falla completes the reference to the addressee, with ll rather than OCR lt. Item introduces the separate lexical sense of offering or giving to someone of high standing.
The recipient is a person of high standing; peßoa has o rather than OCR r. The example begins offering one's life to God, with ta- continuing the Japanese verb on the next row.
Tematçuru completes the Japanese verb. The Portuguese explicitly translates offering one's life to God; retain the distinction between Deus in the Japanese example and Deos in the Portuguese gloss.
Tatemauaxi means enclosing something round about or setting something upright around it. The next rows give barriers and folding screens as examples of the enclosure.

runs.text: algũa couſa aleuantada em terno como portas,

lines.note: The enclosing objects are raised around the space, for example doors. The scan reads em terno, with a clear e; retain that anomaly instead of expected em torno. A separate comma is visible immediately before the right rule after portas and is restored.

Folding screens are another example of the surrounding barrier. Biǒbus is embedded in Portuguese prose; its letters are italic and the accent is a caron, correcting the OCR's fractured font runs and circumflex.
Tatemono denotes an insignia or ornament on a helmet. The geographical qualification on the following row makes this an item of Japanese equipment.
De Iapão completes the Japanese helmet-ornament definition. This short continuation is not part of the following verb about setting objects level.
Tatenarabe means making things equal or level by raising or setting them up. The concise Portuguese Aleuantando igualar is retained without supplying an object not printed in the line.
Tatenauoxi means rebuilding, or dismantling something before remaking it. The initial desmã- continues into desmanchar below, with the nasal abbreviation retained.

runs.text: char, & tornar a fazer de nouo caſas, &c.

lines.note: Char completes the dismantling sense, followed by making houses or similar things anew. This row completes the literal construction meaning before the military example.
Teqiga tatenauoita illustrates the enemy recovering or reforming. The Portuguese subject begins ini-, continued as inimigos on the following row.

runs.text: migos a cobrar animo pera pelejar, ou tornarão

lines.note: Migos completes inimigos. The enemies regained courage to fight, or turned again; the last alternative is completed on the next row rather than left as a separate sense.

runs.text: a virar o roſto aos contrarios.

lines.note: Turning one's face toward the opponents completes the renewed-resistance example. Preserve contrarios as the people opposed, not a contrast between alternative dictionary definitions.
Tatevoqi means placing something upright or leaving it raised. Aleuan- begins the Portuguese participle completed below; preserve the headword's printed v rather than harmonizing it to u.
Tada completes aleuantada, describing the object placed upright. The short row closes Tatevoqi and must not be attached to the following kind of headwear.

runs.text: Certa laya de barrete alto de

lines.note: Tateyeboxi is a particular tall cap. The next row supplies its materials; the Japanese headword retains ye and the Portuguese keeps the historical classifying word laya.
The cap is made from paste, paper, or similar material. This completes Tateyeboxi; the separate word below the column is a catchword, not an additional body row.

Read the catchword as Tate-. The worn middle letter is chosen as t by comparison with the neighbouring Tate- headwords, although its incomplete foot makes it look r-like. The raised terminal mark is a hyphen, not a baseline full stop; the following page was not supplied for confirmation.
